Stage 3 · Reading

The longest night in Lerwick

One town, one Tuesday in January, and a boat built in order to be burned.

🔥⛵
1 · Before you read. A town builds a wooden ship every winter and destroys it in one evening. What would you expect the reason to be?

Choose one and say why. Compare with a partner before you read.Choose one and say why before you read.Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

The longest night in Lerwick

Written for this course, from the Lerwick Up Helly Aa Committee’s own history of the festival and reporting by the BBC and Shetland.org.

1On the last Tuesday in January, the town of Lerwick in Shetland burns a boat. The galley is a replica longship, built over about four months by people who will stand and watch it destroyed. At half past seven a rocket goes up, a thousand torches are lit, and the procession moves off through a crowd of five thousand or more. Half an hour later the guizers form a slow circle round the ship, throw their torches into it, and sing. By ten in the evening there is nothing left of the winter’s work but ash.

2The Norse history behind all this is perfectly real. The islands were settled from Norway more than a thousand years ago; a form of Norse was spoken here for centuries after that, and the settlers left their names on almost every hill and voe. Plenty of families can find ancestors in the parish records, and the descendants of those families still work the same ground. What is not real — or rather, what is a great deal younger than the costumes suggest — is the festival itself.

3Up Helly Aa grew out of tar barrelling, a rough midwinter custom in which squads of young men dragged barrels of burning tar through the streets on sledges, making trouble. Around 1870 a group of young men in the town replaced it with something better organised: a later date, elaborate disguise, and a torchlit parade. The Viking element arrived afterwards, in stages. A first sign of it appears in 1877; the galley itself only in the late 1880s; the title Guizer Jarl, worn by the chief guizer, not until 1906; and a Viking squad in the procession every single year only after the First World War. The ceremony people describe as ancient was established, piece by piece, by Victorians who admired a past they had never seen.

4None of that makes it false. A custom does not have to be old to be genuine; it has to be carried by a community that pays for it, builds it and turns up to it in the rain. Ancestry is not the qualification either. In practice a squad is formed among people who live in the town now — an immigrant of ten years’ standing can carry a torch, and a citizen by descent who moved to Aberdeen in 1998 cannot.

5Living customs also argue with themselves. For roughly 142 years the Lerwick squads were open to men only; women organised the halls, the food and the all-night parties, and a good many of them defended that division firmly. Smaller fire festivals elsewhere in Shetland had female participants far earlier, and one of them appointed a woman as its Jarl in 2015. After a two-year gap caused by the pandemic, the Lerwick committee removed the restriction from the 2023 festival, and the following year the Jarl’s own squad included his daughter and three of his nieces. A tradition that can be amended is not a weaker tradition. It is a working one.

6The other pressure comes from outside. The burning galley is the feature every camera wants, and the procession is now streamed live, which has made a town of seven thousand people known globally. The community has had to decide, more than once, how much of the night belongs to the visitors. So far the answer has been roughly this: the fire is yours to look at, and the twenty-four hours in the halls afterwards, which is where the festival actually lives, are ours.

1 · Read the explanation.
One question, asked before every noun

English makes you answer a question before almost every noun: can my listener already tell which one I mean?

If they can — because it has been mentioned, because there is only one, because the sentence itself identifies it — use the. If they cannot, and you mean one of several, use a or an. If you are not talking about particular examples at all, but about a class of things, use no article with a plural or an uncountable noun.

The cases that catch people out
  • Describing versus identifying. She is the teacher points at one person we know. She is a teacher says what she does. Both are correct; they say different things.
  • General statements take no article. Festivals cost money. Not the festivals, unless you mean particular ones.
  • Uncountable nouns work the same way. Information is free in general; the information you sent is specific.
  • Names. No article with most countries, cities and people. But the with plural or descriptive names: the Netherlands, the United States, the Shetland Islands.
  • Superlatives and ordinals are definite by nature: the oldest, the first.

Two things to watch

1 — No article is a choice, not an accident. Festivals cost money and the festivals cost money are both correct English and mean different things. Leaving the article out makes the statement general.

2 — The does not mean important. It means identifiable. A very important thing mentioned for the first time still takes a.

11 · Read this before the extra practice.
The question the article answers

Before choosing, ask what the noun is doing. a / an introduces one of a kind, or says what sort of thing something is: The town burns a boat · It is a ceremony, not a party · He is a citizen of the town. the says that the reader can identify which one: because it has been mentioned (The galley is burned at ten), because there is only one here (The community decides every year), because something after it makes it specific (the custom of burning boats), or because it is a superlative or an ordinal (the most photographed feature, the first settlers).

No article is a real choice, not an absence. Plural and uncountable nouns take nothing when you mean them in general: Immigrants arrived after the war · History is not the same as tradition. Add the and you narrow it to a particular set: The history of these islands is Norse. That contrast — general against particular — is the single most useful test at B2.

Names, institutions and fixed phrases

Most countries, cities and people take no article: settled from Norway, Lerwick was named by Dutch fishermen. Plural names and a handful of others take the: the Shetland Islands, the Netherlands, the United States.

Institutions split by meaning. Without an article they name the activity: He is at school (as a pupil), in hospital (as a patient), in prison (as a prisoner). With the they name the building: She is at the school (in that building, perhaps to fix the roof). British and American usage differ on hospital, and both are correct in their own variety.

Errors to watch: I am student → a student · The immigrants arrived after the war when you mean immigrants in general → no article · the Norway → Norway · a advice — advice is uncountable, so a piece of advice · the most photographed feature without the is impossible: a superlative always takes it.

1 · Read the model.
Model · an entry for a visitor website

Once a year, on the first Saturday in March, the village of Yelken holds a horse festival. The riders come down from the high pastures the night before, and by dawn there are three hundred horses in a field that is normally empty.

The festival is old, but not as old as visitors assume. The custom of racing in early spring goes back several centuries; the present form, with the ceremony at the well and the parade through the village, was established after the war, when the families who had returned wanted something to mark the first grass.

Photographs are welcome at the parade and at the races, which are the most photographed feature of the day. The ceremony at the well is not open, and we ask visitors to respect that. It lasts eleven minutes and it belongs to the families who lost people.

Come for the horses. Do not come expecting a show: the village is not performing, and there is nowhere to sit.
